title: E-commerce Order System
subtitle: Amazon / Flipkart Checkout Architecture: Saga Orchestration, Striped Flash-Sale Inventory & Immutable Price Snapshots
keyTakeaways: Coordinate distributed checkout across Order, Inventory, Payment, and Fulfillment services using a stateful Saga Orchestrator with explicit compensating transactions (`releaseInventory`, `refundPayment`) and Outbox persistence: never distributed XA two-phase commits across microservices.

Capture an immutable JSON/relational snapshot of item title, merchant ID, unit price, tax rate, and applied promo discount inside `order_items` at the exact moment of checkout so future catalog edits never mutate historical order totals.

Eliminate database row-lock bottlenecks on flash-sale SKUs (e.g., iPhone launch with 100,000 units) by striping inventory across $K = 64$ database sub-buckets (`sku_id#00`.`#63`) combined with an atomic Redis Lua token pre-check.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: An E-commerce Order System (like Amazon, Flipkart, or Shopify Checkout) converts a buyer's shopping cart into a confirmed, paid, and warehouse-routed order while guaranteeing zero overselling and complete auditability across distributed microservices.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Cart-to-Checkout validation: verify item availability, compute item-level tax & shipping, and validate coupon/promo rules; (2) Order creation with immutable price/tax/catalog snapshotting; (3) Atomic inventory reservation with automatic release if payment fails or times out; (4) Distributed checkout orchestration across Inventory, Payment, Promo, and Warehouse Fulfillment services; (5) Order lifecycle tracking (`PENDING_RESERVATION -> RESERVED -> PAID -> FULFILLING -> SHIPPED -> DELIVERED / CANCELLED`) and partial/full cancellations.

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Consistency: Zero overselling of physical inventory and strict eventual consistency (via Saga) across Order, Inventory, and Payment states; (2) Availability: 99.99% on the order placement path; (3) Latency: P99 < 300ms for checkout initiation and inventory reservation; (4) Flash-Sale Resilience: Handle 50,000 concurrent checkout attempts on a single hot launch SKU without locking up the inventory database.
Out of Scope: Product search relevance ranking, recommendation engines, and last-mile delivery truck GPS routing.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: We size the system for a global retail marketplace handling both steady daily shopping and massive Prime Day / Singles' Day flash peaks.
bullets: User Base & Order Volume: 300 Million MAU, 80 Million DAU; 25 Million completed orders per day baseline (averaging 3 line items per order = 75 Million `order_items` per day).
Peak Flash-Sale Multiplier: 15x traffic spike during Prime Day / Black Friday opening hour (~17,000 orders/sec across the platform).
Read-to-Write Ratio: 20:1 (buyers check order status, tracking pages, and order history 20 times for every 1 order placed -> 500 Million order reads/day).
Average Payload Sizes: `orders` header + 3 `order_items` (with immutable price/tax/product snapshot) + `saga_state_log` = 4 KB per order.
Catalog & SKU Footprint: 500 Million active SKUs across 200 regional fulfillment centers.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: We compute baseline and flash-sale QPS, Redis memory for hot SKU inventory counters and active carts, and 5-year sharded order database storage.
bullets: Order Write QPS: 25M orders / 86,400 sec ≈ 290 orders/sec average (~870 `order_items`/sec); Peak Order Write QPS (15x) ≈ 4,350 orders/sec (and up to 15,000 checkout attempts/sec including failed flash-sale attempts).
Order Read QPS: 500M reads / 86,400 sec ≈ 5,787 reads/sec average; Peak Read QPS (15x) ≈ 86,800 reads/sec.

Redis Memory (Active Shopping Carts + Hot SKU Inventory Tokens + Idempotency): (a) 80M DAU active carts × 2 KB = 160 GB; (b) 50M active/hot SKUs cached in Redis (`sku:{id}:stock` + reservation hashes) × 256 bytes = 12.8 GB; (c) 50M checkout idempotency keys (48h TTL) × 256 bytes = 12.8 GB. Total Redis RAM with 2x replication ≈ 372 GB.

5-Year Relational Storage (Orders + Order Items + Saga Audit Log): 25M orders/day × 4 KB = 100 GB/day -> 36.5 TB/year -> 182.5 TB raw over 5 years. With 3x replication and secondary indexes (`buyer_id`, `seller_id`, `created_at`) ≈ 766 TB across sharded PostgreSQL/Vitess/CockroachDB.
Bandwidth: Peak Ingress = 15,000 checkout QPS × 4 KB = 60 MB/sec (480 Mbps); Peak Egress = 86,800 read QPS × 4 KB = 347 MB/sec (2.78 Gbps).

codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
E-COMMERCE ORDER SYSTEM CAPACITY WORKSHEET (25M ORDERS/DAY, 15X FLASH PEAK)
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT (QPS)
   - Avg Order Creation QPS   : 25,000,000 / 86,400         = 290 orders/sec
   - Peak Order Creation (15x): 290 * 15                    = 4,350 orders/sec
   - Peak Checkout Attempts   : ~15,000 QPS (during flash drops)
   - Avg Order Status Read QPS: 500,000,000 / 86,400        = 5,787 QPS
   - Peak Order Read QPS (15x): 5,787 * 15                  = 86,805 QPS

2. REDIS MEMORY (SHOPPING CARTS + HOT SKU INVENTORY + IDEMPOTENCY)
   - Active Carts (80M DAU)   : 80,000,000 * 2 KB           = 160.0 GB
   - Hot SKU Inventory Cache  : 50,000,000 SKUs * 256 B     = 12.8 GB
   - Checkout Idempotency Keys: 50,000,000 keys * 256 B     = 12.8 GB
   - Total Redis Cluster (2x) : 185.6 GB * 2 (Replica)      = 371.2 GB RAM

3. 5-YEAR ORDER DATABASE STORAGE (SHARDED BY BUYER_ID / ORDER_ID)
   - Per-Order Record Size    : 4 KB (Header + 3 Items + Saga Log)
   - Daily Storage Growth     : 25,000,000 * 4 KB           = 100 GB / day
   - 5-Year Raw Storage       : 100 GB * 365 * 5            = 182.5 TB
   - 3x Replicated + Indexes  : 182.5 TB * 3 * 1.4          = 766.5 TB

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Write Ingress       : 15,000 QPS * 4 KB           = 60 MB/s  (480 Mbps)
   - Peak Read Egress         : 86,805 QPS * 4 KB           = 347 MB/s (2.78 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Core external REST/gRPC/WebSocket API contracts, request/response payloads, and underlying storage entities with primary keys (PK), foreign keys (FK), secondary/clustering indexes (IDX), and relationship cardinalities.
bullets: POST /api/v1/orders: Initiates Order Saga (Reserve Inventory -> Charge Payment -> Confirm Order -> Emit Fulfillment Event).
GET /api/v1/orders/{orderId}: Returns current order status, snapshotted item prices, and shipment tracking.
POST /api/v1/orders/{orderId}/cancel: Triggers compensating Saga steps (Refund Payment + Release Reserved Stock).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The E-commerce Order architecture centers on a stateful Saga Orchestrator backed by the Transactional Outbox pattern, coordinating Inventory, Payment, and Warehouse Fulfillment over Kafka.
bullets: Checkout & Order Service (Saga Orchestrator): Snapshots current pricing/tax rules from the Cart & Pricing Service, writes the `orders`, `order_items`, `saga_instances`, and `outbox_events` rows in a single local ACID transaction, and drives the multi-step checkout workflow.

Inventory Service (Redis Token Gate + 64-Way Striped DB): Handles `ReserveInventoryCommand`. First checks/decrements the SKU's Redis token counter via Lua; if successful, persists the reservation in `sku_inventory_buckets` (`bucket_id = hash(orderId) % 64`) with a 15-minute payment TTL.
Payment Service: Processes `ProcessPaymentCommand` idempotently using `orderId` as the payment key. If the card is declined or expires after 15 minutes, emits `PaymentFailedEvent`.

Compensating Transaction Handler: When `PaymentFailedEvent` arrives, the Saga Orchestrator transitions the saga to `COMPENSATE_RELEASE_INVENTORY` and sends `ReleaseInventoryCommand` to restore the reserved stock back to the exact `bucket_id`.

Fulfillment & Order Split Service: Once paid, splits multi-item orders into physical `ShipmentOrder`s grouped by optimal fulfillment center proximity and dispatches pick-pack-ship tasks to the Warehouse Management System (WMS).

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: We trace the two fundamental high-concurrency order pipelines: 64-way striped inventory reservation and orchestrated Saga failure compensation.
bullets: Striped Inventory Reservation (Prevents Hot-Row DB Lock Contention): For viral flash sales, storing inventory in a single row causes catastrophic row-level lock contention. The system stripes available stock across 64 database bucket rows per SKU; incoming orders hash their order ID to decrement a specific bucket (`bucket_id = hash(orderId) % 64`), scaling write throughput 64-fold.

Compensating Saga Orchestration & Rollback: Checkout is coordinated through an Orchestrated Saga. In the happy path, inventory is reserved, payment is captured, and fulfillment is scheduled. If payment fails or times out, the Saga Orchestrator dispatches compensating commands (`ReleaseInventoryCmd`, `RevokePromoRedemptionCmd`), restoring stock and marking the order `CANCELLED_PAYMENT_FAILED`.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Scaling an E-commerce Order System to support millions of third-party sellers and global fulfillment requires dual-sharded projections, bucket rebalancing, and asynchronous tax/fraud pipelines.
bullets: Tail-End Bucket Consolidation for Striped Inventory: When a flash-sale SKU has only 20 units left spread across 64 buckets (e.g., 1 unit in 20 different buckets) and a buyer orders `quantity = 2`, a single-bucket check would fail. Once total Redis remaining stock drops below `2 × NUM_INVENTORY_BUCKETS` (128 units), a lightweight background worker consolidates remaining stock into `bucket_id = 0` so multi-unit orders can still succeed cleanly.

Buyer vs. Seller Dual-Sharded Views (CQRS): Buyers query `GET /orders?buyerId=X` while third-party merchants query `GET /seller/orders?sellerId=Y`. Because a single buyer order can contain items from 3 different sellers, shard the authoritative `orders` table by `buyer_id` (or `order_id`), and stream `OrderItemCreated` events via Kafka into a read-optimized `seller_order_items` table sharded by `seller_id`.

Warehouse Geo-Routing & Order Splitting: If a buyer in Chicago orders 3 items where 2 are in the Illinois fulfillment center and 1 is only available in California, the Fulfillment Service splits the parent `Order` into two child `Shipment` entities after payment capture, minimizing shipping cost and delivery latency.

Abandoned Reservation Reaper: If a buyer reserves inventory at checkout and closes their browser tab without submitting payment, a background Reaper sweeps `inventory_reservations WHERE status = 'RESERVED' AND expires_at < NOW()`, emits `PAYMENT_TIMED_OUT` to the Saga Orchestrator, and restores both the DB bucket stock and Redis token counter.

tradeOffs.option: Saga Orchestration (Central Order Coordinator) vs. Saga Choreography (Peer-to-Peer Events)
tradeOffs.pros: Orchestration centralizes checkout state transitions and compensating rollbacks in one place (`saga_instances`), making timeout handling and debugging straightforward.
tradeOffs.cons: The Order Service must know the command contracts of Inventory, Payment, and Fulfillment services.
tradeOffs.bestFor: E-commerce checkout flows where a multi-step transaction has a clear owner (the Order) and strict rollback ordering.

tradeOffs.option: Reserve Inventory Before Payment vs. Deduct Inventory Only After Payment Capture
tradeOffs.pros: Reserving inventory *before* charging the buyer guarantees you never take a customer's money for an out-of-stock item (zero overselling refunds).
tradeOffs.cons: Requires a 10–15 minute reservation hold TTL and compensating release logic if the buyer abandons payment.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Flash sales, limited-stock physical goods, and high-trust retail marketplaces.

tradeOffs.option: Single SKU Row vs. 64-Way Striped Inventory Buckets
tradeOffs.pros: 64-way striped buckets eliminate database row-lock contention on hot SKUs, increasing single-SKU checkout throughput from ~500 TPS to >30,000 TPS.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires bucket probing or tail-end consolidation when remaining inventory is very low.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Platforms running flash sales, product drops, or high-velocity promotions (Amazon Prime Day, Flipkart Big Billion Days).

interviewTip: When designing an E-commerce Order System, always emphasize two architectural pillars: (1) **Immutable Price & Tax Snapshotting** inside `order_items` (never join `order_items` with the live `products` table to calculate historical order totals!), and (2) **Saga Orchestration with 64-Way Striped Inventory Buckets** so flash-sale SKUs never bottleneck on a single database row lock.
